title: How much memory a 7B model needs
summary: Seven billion parameters take 28 GB as 32-bit numbers, 14 GB as 16-bit and 3.5 GB as 4-bit. That counts the weights only.

beats.say: One model can weigh twenty eight gigabytes or three and a half.
A seven billion parameter model stores seven billion numbers.
How much space each number takes depends on its format.
beats.cap: Space per number depends on format

beats.say: A thirty two bit number takes four bytes. A sixteen bit number takes two.
Seven billion times four bytes is twenty eight gigabytes.
At sixteen bits, that halves to fourteen gigabytes.
At four bits, it drops to three and a half.
Same count of numbers. One eighth of the space.
This counts only the stored weights, not the working memory.
Fewer bits per number trade precision for space.
beats.cap: Fewer bits: less space, less precision

claims.note: NVIDIA mixed precision guide: FP16 uses 16 bits, compared to 32 bits for single precision (FP32)

facts.claim: A single-precision (binary32) number uses 32 bits, which is 4 bytes
facts.note: Wikipedia, Single-precision floating-point format: binary32 under IEEE 754 occupies 32 bits; 8 bits per byte gives 4 bytes

facts.claim: Half precision (FP16) uses 16 bits, compared to 32 bits for single precision
facts.note: NVIDIA, Train With Mixed Precision: 'Half-precision floating point format (FP16) uses 16 bits, compared to 32 bits for single precision (FP32)'

facts.claim: A 1B-parameter model needs about 4 GB at FP32, 2 GB at FP16 and about 0.5 GB at 4-bit, and a 7B model at FP16 is about 14 GB
facts.note: UW-Madison ML-X Nexus, Quantization and Precision: table FP32 32 bits / 4 bytes / 4 GB per 1B; FP16 16 / 2 / 2 GB; INT8 8 / 1 / 1 GB; 4-bit 4 / 0.5 / ~0.5 GB; a 7B model at FP16 is ~14 GB
